strengths: MSAM offers a simple, practically useful modification of momentum optimization: it reuses the existing momentum buffer and requires one forward/backward pass per step. Table 1 supports negligible runtime overhead, reporting relative speed 0.99 versus 0.52 for SAM.

The empirical improvements over base optimizers are meaningful. On CIFAR100, WRN-16-4 improves from 76.90% to 79.11%, close to SAM’s 79.25%. Experiments cover several CNNs and ViTs, adaptive and BatchNorm-only variants, and a small translation experiment.

The ablations provide useful insight beyond the proposed update. Investigations of perturbation sign, normalization, learning-rate scaling, alternative directions, and equal computational budgets help distinguish MSAM from conventional NAG. The importance of decoupling perturbation magnitude from the learning-rate schedule is particularly interesting.

The presentation is generally understandable, with helpful optimizer diagrams, extensive hyperparameter plots, and a code link. Warm-up sensitivity and large-radius instability are discussed candidly. No material ethical concerns are apparent from the reported benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantee has a concrete correctness problem. Proposition 1 is false for negative Hessian trace: with H = diag(-2, 0), standard Gaussian perturbations, and rho = 1, Eq. 9 asserts approximately -0.1804 <= -1. Setting 1 does not exclude this case. Theorem 3 also lacks a sufficient derivation connecting the truncated Gaussian empirical-loss bound to unperturbed population risk, including the necessary assumptions and Taylor-remainder control. These gaps materially undermine the claimed theoretical support.

The main ImageNet comparisons favor MSAM through asymmetric warm-up treatment. MSAM disables perturbations during warm-up, whereas SAM retains them, despite Table A.1 showing that disabling them improves SAM from 69.2% to 69.8%, above MSAM’s 69.1%. The claimed accuracy parity therefore needs reassessment with appropriately tuned warm-up settings for both methods.

Model selection and uncertainty reporting leave important evaluation questions unresolved. Appendix A.6 reports the best perturbation radius alongside test-accuracy search curves, without specifying an independent validation procedure. Most ImageNet results use single runs; variability estimated from the smallest baseline models cannot establish uncertainty for other architectures or optimizers. These issues particularly affect claims based on small accuracy differences.

The broad claim of comparable SAM performance overstates the evidence on larger ViTs. MSAM trails SAM by 2.4 percentage points on ViT-S/16 at 300 epochs and 2.0 points on ViT-B/16 at 90 epochs. Equal-compute comparisons are valuable but cover only WRN-16-4 and ViT-S/32, leaving the tradeoff unresolved for the configurations with the largest deficits.

The mechanistic interpretation remains preliminary. Figure 3 removes gradient components outside the SAM–SGD plane, so projected alignment does not establish similarity of the full gradients. Likewise, the limited directional sharpness measurements do not establish global sharpness minimization. Momentum averages gradients at changing parameter locations, and its proposed interpretation as a better full-dataset gradient approximation needs more direct evidence.

Reproducibility reporting needs completion despite the code link: the manuscript lacks an explicit AdamW update specification, CIFAR seed counts, GPU identification, and per-model wall-clock measurements. Algorithm 1 also requires a convention for normalizing the initially zero momentum vector. The incorrect theory and insufficiently controlled comparisons are the principal reasons for rejection; these reporting omissions are secondary.
